red.focus: Analyze rights claims as structured propositions
red.summary: A legal-rights argument must name who is protected, against whom, and under what conditions. Learn to make the claim clear enough that another person can test it.
checklist: I can identify a claimant and duty holder
I can express a right as a conditional legal proposition
I can avoid confusing a moral hope with an enforceable right

sections.title: Give the Claim a Subject
sections.body_md: A student says, 'I have a right to see my examination records.' An analyst should ask which law, educational institution and type of record are involved. The existence of a right may depend on definitions, deadlines and exceptions. A clear proposition identifies who can demand what from whom and on which conditions. This small step makes the argument testable. Without it, the word right can hide several different claims and remedies.

sections.title: Rights and Duties Are Related
sections.body_md: If a valid law requires an agency to provide specified records to an eligible applicant, the applicant may have a corresponding claim against the agency. The exact legal relationship depends on the rule. Rights can also include liberties, powers or immunities rather than only claims to another person's action. At a beginner level, start by naming the protection and any corresponding obligation without treating all rights as identical. This prevents mistaken assumptions about who must act.

sections.title: Check the Exception
sections.body_md: The same records rule may protect confidential information about other people. An argument asserting complete access without reading the exceptions may be invalid under the governing law. A precise conclusion follows only after eligibility, covered documents, exemptions and procedures are examined. Logical clarity is not coldness; it helps a student understand why a request succeeds or fails and which lawful step may protect the person's interests.

yellow.focus: Use correlatives to analyze competing legal positions
yellow.summary: Learn why a claim right, liberty, power and immunity describe different legal relationships. Apply the distinctions to a practical dispute without treating them as interchangeable.
checklist: I can distinguish claim from liberty
I can identify a legal power that changes relations
I can recognize an immunity protecting against another's power

sections.title: Four Ways a Right May Operate
sections.body_md: Wesley Hohfeld's framework distinguishes claim rights, liberties, powers and immunities. A claim right corresponds to another's duty. A liberty means one lacks a duty to refrain from a specified act, not that every other person must assist. A power permits a person to change legal relations, such as through a valid contractual offer or appointment in defined circumstances. An immunity protects a person against another's ability to alter a legal position. These distinctions make legal argument more exact.
sections.audio_script: Wesley Hohfeld's framework distinguishes claim rights, liberties, powers and immunities. A claim right corresponds to another's duty. A liberty means one lacks a duty to refrain from a specified act, not that every other person must assist. A power permits a person to change legal relations, such as through a valid contractual offer or appointment in defined circumstances. An immunity protects a person against another's ability to alter a legal position. These distinctions make legal argument more exact.

sections.title: Liberty Is Not a Demand for Assistance
sections.body_md: A person may have a liberty to speak in a public forum under applicable law but not a right to compel a private newspaper to publish the speech. The two relations involve different duty holders and limits. Confusing them can turn a sound freedom argument into an unsupported affirmative claim. A lawyer should specify the exact conduct, party and source before reasoning about which correlative duties exist. This method is especially useful in constitutional and contract disputes.

A lawyer should specify the exact conduct, party and source before reasoning about which correlative duties exist. This method is especially useful in constitutional and contract disputes.

sections.title: Legal Powers Change Relationships
sections.body_md: A person with capacity to enter a valid contract may alter the parties' rights and duties by accepting an offer. That is a legal power, not simply a liberty to think about an agreement. An institution may also have power to issue lawful orders, while another person has immunity from certain changes. An element chart should distinguish which actor holds which position. Precise legal relationships reduce semantic confusion and make questions about consent and authority easier to answer.

orange.focus: Resolve rights conflicts by separating different logical relations
orange.summary: Advanced disputes can involve a liberty for one actor and a claim by another. Analyze the relationships precisely before attempting proportionality or policy balancing.
checklist: I can map multiple rights and duty holders
I can identify mistaken equivalences in rights language
I can explain how exceptions change legal relations

sections.title: Different Claims Can Pass Each Other
sections.body_md: A journalist may have freedom against state censorship while a private person has a privacy claim concerning certain disclosures. These positions involve different actors and sources. The fact that the journalist possesses one liberty does not prove the absence of every duty to the person whose information might be published. Before balancing, identify each party, the corresponding legal position and any applicable statutory or constitutional limits. Otherwise an apparent conflict may be created simply by imprecise vocabulary.

Otherwise an apparent conflict may be created simply by imprecise vocabulary.

sections.title: Analyze the Legal Power to Restrict
sections.body_md: A regulator may possess a legal power to issue safety rules while citizens hold rights constraining that power. An individual's immunity can mean the regulator lacks authority to alter a protected position in specified ways. An argument about 'government power' therefore needs to specify what act is authorized and what legal constraints apply. Hohfeldian language can expose gaps, though it does not by itself resolve the moral priority between competing interests.
sections.audio_script: A regulator may possess a legal power to issue safety rules while citizens hold rights constraining that power. An individual's immunity can mean the regulator lacks authority to alter a protected position in specified ways. An argument about 'government power' therefore needs to specify what act is authorized and what legal constraints apply. Hohfeldian language can expose gaps, though it does not by itself resolve the moral priority between competing interests.

sections.title: Exceptions Can Alter the Relationship
sections.body_md: A person may ordinarily have a claim to confidential treatment but consent to a narrow disclosure. The effect of consent depends on applicable law; it may waive a claim, supply a defense, or change another legal relation. A sophisticated analysis identifies the exact consequence rather than saying consent always removes all rights. Logical precision becomes a practical tool for protecting individuals from overbroad interpretations of permissions they gave for limited purposes.

black.focus: Critique rights analysis beyond formal correlatives
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate how a formally precise rights map may still hide social inequality, institutional power or uncertainty about whose interests count. Connect analytical clarity with justice.
checklist: I can apply legal-relations analysis without erasing context
I can evaluate distribution of legal powers and immunities
I can defend rights adjudication under disagreement

sections.title: Precision Is Necessary but Not Sufficient
sections.body_md: Hohfeldian analysis can identify that an employer has a legal power to change certain conditions while a worker lacks a corresponding immunity under current law. That is a descriptive clarification, not necessarily a moral endorsement. A doctoral scholar should distinguish the existing legal relation from a normative argument that the allocation of power is unfair. This prevents two mistakes: confusing advocacy for reform with current law and assuming an accurate legal classification answers every question of justice.

sections.title: Formal Symmetry Can Hide Dependence
sections.body_md: Two parties may both have legal liberty to end a contract, but one may have far fewer practical alternatives. A purely formal map records the same type of legal position while overlooking different effects. A mature analysis examines how information, vulnerability and mandatory protections shape whether apparent freedoms are meaningful. Law may appropriately create additional claims or immunities to protect persons in unequal relationships. The argument must specify the legal mechanism and its costs.

sections.title: Rights Require Institutions to Be Real
sections.body_md: A claim right against a state agency may be clear in principle but difficult to enforce without legal aid, translated forms or timely review. A doctoral theory should evaluate the route from right through duty to actual remedy. It should also respect the agency's lawful authority and other people's rights. Analytical rigor and human concern belong together: knowing exactly what a person can demand is valuable only when the legal system gives them a meaningful path to protection.
